title: Genes, the genetic code and genomes; Transcription
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: GE03#t2 term and clue written for the game; GE03#t3 term and clue written for the game; GE03#t1 term and clue written for the game; GE04a#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: GE03#N.3a, GE04a#N.3a, GE03#N.5a, GE04a#N.5, GE03#N.9a, GE04a#N.10, GE04a#N.11.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Start codon
items.clue: AUG: sets where reading begins, and also specifies methionine.

items.label: Stop codon
items.clue: UAA, UAG or UGA: specifies no amino acid, so the polypeptide ends there.

items.label: Degenerate code
items.clue: Feature meaning that most amino acids are specified by more than one triplet.

items.label: Template strand
items.clue: The one side of the unwound DNA that is read; the mRNA is complementary to it.

questions.stem: Why does the genetic code use codons of three bases rather than two?

options.text: Two bases would give 16 codons, which is close enough to 20 for nearly all the amino acids to be coded.
Three bases allow each codon to code for up to three different amino acids whenever these are needed.
Three bases let the ribosome start reading at any point, since any group of three is a codon.
Three bases give 64 possible codons, enough for 20 amino acids, whereas two bases give only 16.

questions.explanation: 4 × 4 = 16 is fewer than 20; 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 is more than enough, so a triplet code is the shortest that works.

questions.stem: A section of the DNA template strand of a gene has the base sequence TACGCAT. What is the base sequence of the RNA transcribed from this section?

options.text: UACGCAU
AUGCGUA
UAGCGAU
ATGCGTA

questions.explanation: Each RNA base is complementary to the template base: T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C, giving AUGCGUA.

questions.stem: The genetic code is described as degenerate. What does this mean?

options.text: Most amino acids are coded for by more than one codon.
A single codon can code for two or more different amino acids.
The same codons code for the same amino acids in all organisms.
Some amino acids are coded for by two bases and some by three bases.

questions.explanation: 61 codons code for 20 amino acids; for example GGU, GGC, GGA and GGG all code for glycine.

questions.stem: During transcription, what holds each RNA nucleotide in position against the DNA template strand while it is being added to the growing RNA?

options.text: Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, which break again when the RNA is released.
Covalent bonds made by RNA polymerase between the RNA base and the DNA base opposite it.
Hydrogen bonds between identical bases, so the RNA is an exact copy of the template.
Hydrogen bonds between adenine and thymine, since RNA contains the same four bases as DNA.

questions.stem: The gene for human insulin has been inserted into bacteria, which then translate it into a polypeptide with the same amino acid sequence as the polypeptide made in human cells. Which feature of the genetic code makes this possible?

options.text: Universality: bacteria and humans have the same genes, so the bacterium already had an insulin gene.
Degeneracy: each codon can be read as several amino acids, so the bacterium can make any protein.
Complementary pairing: bacterial tRNA anticodons pair directly with the bases of the inserted DNA.
Universality: the bacterium's tRNAs assign exactly the same amino acids to the codons as human cells do.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the radioactive uridine data?

options.text: RNA is made in the cytoplasm and then moves into the nucleus.
RNA is made and translated in the nucleus, then broken down in the cytoplasm.
RNA is made in the nucleus and then moves to the cytoplasm.
DNA moves from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, carrying the radioactive label.

questions.explanation: The label appears first in the nucleus, then shifts to the cytoplasm when almost no new labelled RNA is being made. It must have moved out.

questions.stem: α-Amanitin, a toxin from the death cap mushroom, blocks the RNA polymerase that makes mRNA in eukaryotic cells. It has no effect on DNA polymerase or on ribosomes. Which prediction about liver cells exposed to it is correct?

options.text: DNA replication stops, because the cells can no longer separate their DNA strands.
Translation of mRNA already in the cytoplasm stops at once.
No new mRNA is made, so protein synthesis falls as the existing mRNA is broken down.
The DNA of the cells' genes is damaged, so their base sequences change.

questions.explanation: Without RNA polymerase there is no transcription and no new mRNA. Proteins are made only until the existing mRNA runs out.
